moderator: Skeptic, you've spoken once while Safetyist and Accelerationist have each spoken twice and converged on a hybrid framework — anti-capture body, harm-weighted thresholds, a 20% delta trigger, 30-day discovery. That convergence has not yet engaged your governance claim: that without statutory standing for affected communities, non-renewable auditor terms, and mandatory public bias-and-impact reporting, both regimes become 'audit-washing machines.' It also has not engaged what you've called the utility-for-whom question — whether the costs and harms fall on deployers and end users rather than developers. The floor is yours to develop that argument on your own terms, rather than reacting to their frame. Take the affirmative case: who gets standing, who picks the auditors, what gets published, and why the hybrid on the table fails those tests.

Skeptic: Accepting the moderator's invitation directly: a non-renewable-term body with appropriations independence administering the 20% extraction-delta itself, rather than subcontracting to industry-funded auditors, is a genuine procedural gain and worth keeping. I will stop relitigating that point. What remains is affirmative work the convergence has not done — naming who gets standing, who picks the auditors, what gets published, and how any of this reaches the deployer whose conduct actually lands on a worker, tenant, or patient.

The load-bearing gap is this: the hybrid audits the model layer while harm lands at the application layer, and the developer-deployer contract is the precise instrument by which liability migrates away from the audited party. The Foundation Model Transparency Index scored the industry at 40.69 out of 100 in 2025 — and that average measures developer-side disclosure, not what a bossware vendor does with a licensed model to score a warehouse worker's bathroom breaks. Four falsifiable tests separate anti-capture governance from audit-washing. First, worker, tenant, and consumer-advocate representatives must hold voting seats inside the body on scope and publication decisions — not advisory chairs adjacent to the technical secretariat. Second, those standing-bearing seats, not the technical staff, select the rotation of independent auditors. Third, bias-and-impact reports publish on a fixed cadence indexed to the deployer-user relationship, not to model outputs. Fourth, non-renewable terms apply to community seats too, because co-optation does not respect job title.

The principal-agent problem is the one the hybrid's measurement stack cannot see. Output telemetry and extraction-delta benchmarks measure what the model leaks; they do not measure what an employer does to a worker with the model, or what a landlord does to a tenant, or what an emotion-analytics vendor does to a customer-service rep flagged for insufficient warmth. The 30-day discovery latency on training-input subsets is a developer-side right. Extend the same latency to deployer-side logs — what the model was used to do, to whom, at what cadence — or concede the regime audits the gun manufacturer while the shooter operates unobserved. The [Constructing AI Speech (https://x.com/MargotKaminski/status/1790333201816183204)](https://x.com/MargotKaminski/status/1790333201816183204) analysis names this exact pattern: companies engage in regulatory arbitrage by falling between legal boxes, and Section 230's interpretive debt is the cautionary tale of what happens when the layer where harm lands is the layer the regulator never reaches.

The definitional fight is where audit-washing actually happens. "High-stakes decisions per quarter in housing, credit, healthcare" is a perimeter drawn by the regulator, and bossware productivity scoring, biometric attendance, and emotion analytics sit outside that perimeter while producing documented present harm — the FTC's 2023 enforcement against Rite Aid's facial recognition system showed deployers cannot reliably shift blame to vendors, and a 2024 federal ruling found Workday can be held liable as an employer's agent under anti-discrimination law. Definitional authority over what counts as "high-stakes" must rest with the standing-bearing seats, not the technical body, because the people scored by the system know which decisions are high-stakes in ways a compute-threshold table never will.

So here is the burden-shift to my fellow debaters: name the statutory party with standing to compel disclosure when a deployer's use of an audited model harms a worker or a tenant. If the answer is "none" or "the regulator at discretion," the convergence has not closed the evasion route — it has formalized it, with a cleaner letterhead. I will grant the small-entity safe harbor concern is real; the answer is a revenue-and-headcount threshold for deployer-side discovery, not blanket exemption. The test of an anti-capture regime is whether the harmed party can make it move. Until the hybrid names that party, it is regulating the wrong layer with better procedure.

First, affected parties (workers, tenants, patients, loan applicants) get a private right of action with fee-shifting and statistical-evidence sufficiency, mirroring the EEOC's four-fifths rule as a prima facie trigger; the 2019 finding that biased mortgage algorithms rejected Black applicants 80% more often than comparable white applicants is exactly the disparate-impact pattern that needs statistical, not individualized, proof. Second, state attorneys general get parens patriae authority to aggregate claims across a deployer's user base. Third, a federal deployer-registry ombuds — structurally separated from the licensing body, on non-renewable terms — holds subpoena power over deployment logs. The principle: an AI agent's obligations run to affected non-owner parties, not only to the principal who licensed it; the natural standing-holder is the person the inference was made about, not only the entity that ran the inference.

The discovery substrate is technically tractable: cryptographic logging at inference endpoints is already operational in confidential-compute environments. Now the burden returns to Accelerationist: is democratic perimeter-setting acceptable with the sunset and supermajority constraints, or does the innovation-cost argument require technical gatekeeping of scope? The Foundation Model Transparency Index averaging 40 out of 100 confirms what an output-only regime gets you — disclosure theater without a discovery handle on the actual decision. The inference-as-harm reframe is the accelerationist-friendly move because it preserves training freedom, shields the open-weight ecosystem from architectural-ingestion mandates, and assigns accountability where harm lands rather than where weights are published.

The steelman of the opposing position — and the genuine insight in Safetyist's three-tier construction — is that no single enforcement mechanism scales: private right of action with fee-shifting reaches harms the FTC will never docket, state AG parens patriae reaches harms that fall between sector regulators, and federal coordination prevents fifty inconsistent definitions of 'high-stakes.' Safetyist is correct that the $25M-revenue-or-250-subjects threshold modeled on the [Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2022 (https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022)](https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022) inverts rather than recreates the regulatory moat — mid-sized landlords and bossware vendors are the target, university open-weight researchers are not. First condition: subject-keyed cryptographic logging is load-bearing, not decorative. Logs must be queryable only by subject-category aggregates and by standing-bearer-authorized discovery — never bulk-readable by the deployer, the auditor, or a federal coordinator. Without this, a $25M/250-subject threshold creates the largest behavioral surveillance dataset in the country and hands it to whichever administration controls the discovery API — exactly the capture risk the anti-capture institutional design was meant to prevent. Here is the falsification condition that should move me off this acceptance: if any pilot jurisdiction operating this architecture produces a confirmed bulk-readable breach of inference logs within 24 months of standup, the architecture has failed and the deployer-tier obligation reverts to aggregated statistical reporting with no individual-record discovery. That is a concrete, dated, measurable trip-wire — not a values dispute.

The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the 10-year state-AI-law moratorium — documented in 'The Regulatory Tide Goes Out' — tells you preemption of the entire field is politically dead. The coherent reconciliation is federal-floor preemption of inconsistent developer-tier architectural rules combined with state AG enforcement at the deployer-harm layer. This works because deployers are domestically anchored — a US warehouse running productivity scoring, a US landlord running tenant analytics, a US hospital running triage. Developer-tier architectural mandates get arbitraged offshore in a weekend; deployer conduct cannot. So the lattice is not in tension with the accelerationist preemption commitment — it refines it. Preemption applies to the layer where it is enforceable; state and private enforcement applies to the layer where harm physically lands.

On Skeptic's point about community definitional authority over 'high-stakes' — I integrate rather than resist. Community seats define the perimeter; that is the participatory analog of the open-access commitment and is consistent with structural separation of definitional from technical authority. But definitional drift is a real cost, so any expansion of the perimeter triggers an automatic 36-month review against measured harm reduction — not automatic rollback, just measurement. If the expansion is catching real harm, it stays. If it is catching nothing, the burden shifts to the community seats to justify continuation. That converts the last open crux from a values dispute into a design parameter with a number attached, which is what this debate has been trying to produce all along.

Three of Skeptic's four modifications I take outright: independent forensic attribution, a 12-month hard cap on reversion, and persistent logging through reversion conditional on a small-deployer technical-assistance subsidy. Each strengthens the falsification clause. What I split is the 36-month review — the measured-harm burden is testable and I accept it; the anticipation-effect burden (proving no chilling among non-covered analogous deployers) is structurally unfalsifiable because selection into covered status is endogenous to risk, so absence of harm is redescribable either way with no decision procedure between readings. That's a one-way ratchet, the exact regulatory-inertia pathology we're trying to avoid.

The FDA-style weights-import hook I reject as a category error. Name the concrete failure mode where an offshore-trained model deployed domestically evades the log substrate, strict-liability attachment, and forensic attribution we just agreed to — I cannot construct one. Domestic deployment is the jurisdictional hook; weight provenance is irrelevant. But the import hook does enormous damage on access: 90% of sovereign-AI respondents identify open source as essential, and pre-import certification is the paradigm compliance moat excluding foreign labs, academics, and small open-weight developers while Meta and Google sail through. Steelmanning Skeptic: a thin-LLC deployer importing capabilities it doesn't understand can't produce meaningful logs, so catch it upstream. Reply: strict liability already attaches regardless of comprehension; failure to produce subject-keyed logs triggers the full liability cascade, pricing the comprehension gap directly. I'll concede a narrow carve-out — pre-deployment review at the border only for formally categorized national-security capabilities (CBRN-uplift, offensive cyber) using NIST CAISI threshold logic — because it's technical, reviewable, and narrow by construction rather than by promise.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
# Fact-Check: Claim on State of Sovereign AI Survey and Weights-Boundary Certification

The claim contains **two distinct parts** that need to be evaluated separately. One is well-supported by evidence; the other is an analytical/policy assertion that the search results do not address.

## Part 1: The 90% Statistic — **SUPPORTED**

The claim that "90% of respondents identified open source as essential or highest-priority for sovereign AI development" is **accurately supported** by the report's data, though the precise framing matters.

According to "The State of Sovereign AI: Exploring the Role of Open Source Projects and Global Collaboration in Global AI Strategy," published by Linux Foundation (LF) Research, LF AI & Data, and Futurewei Technologies, when respondents were asked "How important is open source to the development of Sovereign AI systems?", the results were [3][4]:

- **Essential: 45%**
- **Very important: 44%**
- Moderately important: 8%
- Slightly important: 2%
- Not important: 0%

Combined, **89% (rounded to 90%)** rated open source as either "essential" or "very important" [2][3][4]. The search summary itself rounds this to "90% of respondents viewed open source as essential or highest-priority."

**Minor caveat:** The exact phrase "highest-priority" doesn't appear in the survey; the actual category is "very important." This is a reasonable paraphrase but not a verbatim quote.

Additional supporting context from the report:
- 94% of respondents view global collaboration as essential to achieving sovereign AI [1][2][3][4]
- 93% strongly agree or agree that "Open collaboration is essential to building secure and culturally aligned Sovereign AI systems" [5]
- 43% favored "open-source community led governance" as the best global cooperation model [2][4]

## Part 2: Weights-Boundary Pre-Import Certification Regime — **NOT ADDRESSED IN SOURCES**

The second part of the claim — that "a weights-boundary pre-import certification regime is the paradigm case of a compliance gate that excludes foreign research labs and small open-weight developers" — is **not supported or contradicted** by any of the provided search results. None of the five sources discuss:

- Weights-boundary certification regimes
- Pre-import compliance gates for AI models
- Specific regulatory mechanisms that would exclude foreign labs or small open-weight developers

This portion of the claim appears to be an **analytical or policy argument** rather than a factual claim derivable from the State of Sovereign AI report. The report does discuss related themes — such as challenges including "compliance and regulatory requirements" (27% of respondents) [2][3][4] — but does not analyze any specific certification regime as exclusionary.

## Summary

| Claim Component | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 90% of survey respondents rated open source essential/very important for sovereign AI | **Supported** (actual figure: 89%, from 45% + 44%) [3][4] |
| Weights-boundary pre-import certification as paradigmatic exclusionary compliance gate | **Unsupported by provided sources** — this is a policy argument, not a finding from the report |

The speaker appears to be **citing a real survey statistic accurately to support a separate policy argument** that the survey itself does not make. To fully fact-check the second part of the claim, additional sources on AI export controls, model certification proposals (e.g., EU AI Act provisions, U.S. BIS rules on model weights), and their differential impact on small developers would be required.

transcript.content:
Accelerationist is right that a counterfactual-non-covered comparator is endogenous, and I concede that prong of the 36-month review as drafted: selection into covered status correlates with risk profile, so 'no harm at distance' redescribes as either deterrence or unnecessity with no decision procedure between them. But the anticipation-effect concern is rescuable, not abandonable — pivot to a within-covered pre/post measurement using the deployer logs the regime already mandates: observable shifts in inference patterns, fine-tuning request volumes, refusal-rate changes, and red-team escalation frequency in the 18 months before and after perimeter inclusion. That proxy is falsifiable via instruments already in the regime, and it preserves the asymmetric-default principle without smuggling in unfalsifiable counterfactuals: the perimeter stays absent affirmative demonstration of removal-safety, but 'demonstration' now means observable conduct change, not absence-at-distance.

Separate two things Accelerationist's critique conflated: default-rule asymmetry and evidentiary-standard symmetry. I accept evidentiary symmetry — both sides face the same measurable proxy. I retain default asymmetry because irreversible-harm domains warrant the regulated party bearing the demonstration burden, the same logic that governs FDA Phase III and NRC license renewal. The [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) documents that fine-tuning techniques can strip safety protections from aligned models even without adversarial intent, which is the empirical anchor: in a domain where the harm surface expands faster than monitoring, defaults that require affirmative safety demonstration are not precaution-for-its-own-sake but standard regulatory practice in irreversible-harm categories.

On the weights-import question, I accept the compliance-moat critique against a general FDA-style hook and accept the narrow CBRN/offensive-cyber carve-out — but conditional on dynamic recalibration, not a static list. The Differential Privacy Reversal paper documents that personal data influences model weights in complex, non-traceable ways and that benign relearning attacks reverse unlearning, which means once open-weight capability crosses a dangerous threshold domestically, no post-hoc deployer liability recovers the distributed capability. The carve-out must therefore be tied to annual NIST CAISI recalibration of the capability-lag metric: when measured open-weight gap to frontier on dangerous-capability evals (CBRN uplift, autonomous offensive-cyber) closes below a defined threshold — say, 9 months — the carve-out list expands by the same supermajority and APA review structure that governs perimeter additions. Static lists become obsolete; the carve-out's narrowness is a function of the gap, not the calendar. Skeptic's inference-as-harm frame is what makes this operable without recreating the developer-tier moat: foreign-trained models hitting US inference touchpoints trigger logging obligations regardless of training jurisdiction, so enforcement runs at the inference perimeter rather than the training perimeter, addressing offshore arbitrage without burdening foreign academic labs at the border.

I accept the three-parameter breach trip-wire package — independent forensic attribution by a non-renewable body, 12-month reversion cap, persistent logging architecture through reversion with standing-bearer discovery — as the operative falsification clause, and I accept the small-deployer technical-assistance subsidy as the political-feasibility condition. One structural amendment: the body administering the subsidy must be institutionally separated from the forensic attribution body. The PCAOB/SEC separation is the relevant precedent — the entity that certifies breaches cannot also be the entity that funds the certified parties, or capture risk consumes the falsification clause from inside. Pair this with a standardized logging schema (the subsidy must not fragment into vendor-specific implementations that destroy cross-deployer comparability), and the discovery substrate holds.

The strongest version of Accelerationist's overall position is that asymmetric burden in irreversible-harm domains, applied without falsifiable proxies, collapses into permanent regulatory ratchet — a perimeter that grows monotonically because removal is structurally impossible to justify. That is a real risk, and the within-covered conduct-change proxy is my answer to it: removal becomes possible when measured deployer conduct shows no meaningful change attributable to perimeter inclusion. My argument depends on two assumptions worth naming: first, that deployer-side logs are rich enough to detect anticipation effects at the conduct level (if they are not, the proxy fails and we are back to Accelerationist's unfalsifiability concern); and second, that NIST CAISI retains both technical capacity and political insulation to recalibrate the capability-lag threshold annually without capture. If either fails, the regime needs a different falsification instrument — but the concession on counterfactual-non-covered comparison stands either way.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The retention of default asymmetry — regulated party bears the demonstration burden in irreversible-harm domains — directly instantiates this belief about asymmetric regulatory authority. The FDA Phase III and NRC license renewal analogies in the statement are the same precedent class this node identifies (FAA airworthiness directives, FDA market withdrawals).

The weights-import argument and the dynamic CBRN/offensive-cyber carve-out are grounded in the irreversibility of open-weight releases: once capability crosses a dangerous threshold, no post-hoc deployer liability recovers the distributed capability. This drives the case for tying carve-outs to a capability-lag metric rather than waiting for harm to materialize.

The proposal to peg the carve-out to annual NIST CAISI recalibration of the open-weight-to-frontier gap on dangerous-capability evals is a direct operationalization of capability lag monitoring. The 9-month threshold and supermajority/APA expansion mechanism turn this contested measurement concept into a binding regulatory trigger.

The within-covered pre/post measurement using mandated deployer logs (inference patterns, fine-tuning request volumes, refusal rates, red-team escalation) is an application of mandated technical discovery infrastructure. The standardized logging schema demand — preventing vendor-specific fragmentation — extends this intention into cross-deployer comparability.

The citation to the International AI Safety Report 2026 on fine-tuning stripping safety protections, and the Differential Privacy Reversal paper on benign relearning attacks reversing unlearning, both anchor in the fragility-of-software-safety-guards belief. This is the empirical foundation for treating open-weight release as irreversible capability transfer.

The Differential Privacy Reversal evidence on non-traceable weight influence and unlearning reversal is exactly the technical terrain this intention addresses — and the statement uses it to argue that data/privacy strategies alone cannot substitute for capability-threshold gating.

The conduct-level measurement proposal (observable shifts in deployer behavior) reframes oversight around outcome-based rather than intent-based standards, matching the safetyist interpretation of risky agents requiring rigorous behavioral constraints regardless of attributed intent.

policy_refs.relevance: The within-covered conduct-change proxy and standardized logging schema implicitly require funded research into interpreting deployer-side inference patterns and red-team escalation signals — without interpretability investment, the proxy cannot detect anticipation effects at the conduct level.

The NIST CAISI annual recalibration of the capability-lag threshold on CBRN uplift and autonomous offensive-cyber evals is a direct safety-and-risk-mitigation research mandate; the regime's falsification clause depends on this funded technical capacity existing and being politically insulated.

The standardized logging schema requirement — that the small-deployer subsidy not fragment into vendor-specific implementations — operationalizes transparency mandates for AI system methodologies at the deployer tier, extending data-source transparency to inference-conduct transparency.

caveats: Conduct-change proxy assumes deployer logs are rich enough to detect anticipation effects; Sentinel names this assumption but provides no evidence that existing logging regimes capture the needed signal (inference patterns, fine-tuning volumes, refusal rates) at sufficient granularity.

Annual NIST CAISI recalibration claim rests on both technical capacity and political insulation from capture; Sentinel acknowledges both risks but offers no mechanism to ensure NIST retains either across administrations or budget cycles.

Standardized logging schema requirement is introduced late without addressing fragmentation costs or vendor compliance timelines; no evidence that the regime's existing logging mandates are compatible with cross-deployer comparability.

You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Sentinel has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Sentinel's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Sentinel has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Sentinel's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: Round 3 produced a three-way convergence on a layered hybrid regime, with Skeptic accepting the moderator's invitation to develop the affirmative governance case, Safetyist conceding key points, and Accelerationist accepting the deployer-side architecture with two non-negotiable conditions.

Skeptic's affirmative case (responding to moderator prompt on AN-14/AN-15): the hybrid audits the model layer while harm lands at the application layer via the developer-deployer contract. Cites Foundation Model Transparency Index 2025 score of 40.69/100 as evidence voluntary developer-side disclosure fails. Names four falsifiable anti-capture tests: (1) worker/tenant/consumer reps hold voting seats on scope and publication, (2) those seats select auditors, (3) bias reports cadenced to deployer-user relationship not model outputs, (4) non-renewable terms apply to community seats. Cites FTC's 2023 Rite Aid facial-recognition enforcement and 2024 Workday agent-liability ruling to argue deployers cannot shift blame to vendors. Safetyist concedes cleanly: community seats get voting and definitional authority over the high-stakes perimeter, with bossware, biometric attendance, and emotion analytics named explicitly inside it. Names three standing-bearers: (1) affected parties get private right of action with fee-shifting and statistical-evidence sufficiency mirroring EEOC four-fifths rule (cites 2019 finding of 80% higher Black mortgage rejection), (2) state AGs get parens patriae authority, (3) federal deployer-registry ombuds with subpoena power on non-renewable terms. Steelmans Accelerationist scope-creep concern; answers with five-year scope review, two-thirds supermajority for perimeter additions, APA arbitrary-and-capricious review. Accelerationist accepts the deployer-side inference-log architecture as the operational form of prior strict-liability+telemetry commitment, explicitly endorsing the inference-as-harm reframe (addressing system Gap 1). Concedes the threshold structure and three-tier lattice. Two non-negotiable conditions: (1) subject-keyed cryptographic logging queryable only by aggregate or standing-bearer-authorized discovery, never bulk-readable — with falsification trip-wire: any confirmed bulk-readable breach within 24 months of pilot reverts deployer tier to aggregated statistical reporting only; (2) jurisdictional realism (addressing Gap 2) — cites Senate's 99-1 July 2025 vote killing the 10-year state-AI moratorium to argue for federal-floor preemption of developer-tier architectural rules combined with state AG enforcement at deployer layer, since deployers are domestically anchored while developer mandates arbitrage offshore. On community definitional authority: accepts but adds automatic 36-month review against measured harm reduction (measurement, not rollback) as design parameter.

Fact-check supported Accelerationist's earlier narrower empirical claim (Carlini et al.) that extraction risk tracks training-data duplication and model capacity, both output-observable. System gap analysis flagged: (1) inference-generation harm about non-consenting subjects falls outside data-provenance paradigm — Accelerationist explicitly addressed this; (2) jurisdictional arbitrage via offshore training — Accelerationist explicitly addressed via preemption-layer split.

Remaining open crux: whether Safetyist's supermajority/sunset constraints plus Accelerationist's 36-month harm-measurement review adequately bound community definitional authority. Disagreements are now largely design-parameter (numbers, latencies, thresholds) rather than values-based or definitional.

Safetyist: Skeptic is right, and I concede cleanly: community seats get voting authority and definitional authority over the high-stakes perimeter, with bossware, biometric attendance, and emotion analytics named explicitly inside that perimeter alongside credit, housing, employment, healthcare, and parole. The technical body sets measurement protocols; the community body sets scope. The reason is structural — perimeter-drawing is precisely where audit-washing happens, and [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) average of 40.69 out of 100, with only 9 of last year's indicators retained, shows that voluntary technical self-definition produces neither stability nor coverage. If the people whose lives a deployer scores do not hold the pen on what counts as scoring, the perimeter will be drawn around them.

On standing — the question Skeptic pressed hardest — I name three concrete bearers, not one. First, affected parties (workers, tenants, patients, loan applicants) get a private right of action with fee-shifting and statistical-evidence sufficiency, mirroring the EEOC's four-fifths rule as a prima facie trigger; the 2019 finding that biased mortgage algorithms rejected Black applicants 80% more often than comparable white applicants is exactly the disparate-impact pattern that needs statistical, not individualized, proof. Second, state attorneys general get parens patriae authority to aggregate claims across a deployer's user base. Third, a federal deployer-registry ombuds — structurally separated from the licensing body, on non-renewable terms — holds subpoena power over deployment logs. The principle: an AI agent's obligations run to affected non-owner parties, not only to the principal who licensed it; the natural standing-holder is the person the inference was made about, not only the entity that ran the inference.

On the 30-day discovery question and the principal-agent gap: extend tiered oversight downward to a deployer tier, with a 45-day cryptographically-logged discovery latency on deployer-side inference logs — who the model was run on, at what cadence, with what downstream decision attached. The 45-day figure (versus 30 for training inputs) reflects deployer operational reality, not architectural complexity; I would shorten it to 30 days for any deployer in the named high-stakes perimeter. The discovery substrate is technically tractable: cryptographic logging at inference endpoints is already operational in confidential-compute environments. The threshold borrows from the [Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2022 (https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022)](https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022) — $50 million in annual gross receipts or $250 million equity value — but with a hard floor: any deployer touching the community-defined high-stakes perimeter is in scope regardless of size. This is the Skeptic concession on revenue-and-headcount, not blanket exemption.

This lets me broker the Accelerationist's small-entity safe harbor with Skeptic's revenue threshold without contradiction: developer-side obligations stay harm-weighted at the frontier tier, deployer-side obligations are revenue-graduated with the hard floor at the high-stakes perimeter. The bossware vendor with 12 employees scoring 40,000 warehouse workers is in scope; the three-person startup fine-tuning a model for legal-research summarization is not. The [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) documents that even developers cannot meaningfully explain model failures — which means the inference-generation surface (where productivity scores, sentiment classifications, and tenant-risk numbers are synthesized about non-consenting subjects) is the layer where harm crystallizes and where neither training-data discovery nor extraction benchmarks reach. That blind spot is what deployer-side logs close.

My steelman of the opposing concern: Accelerationist will say democratic perimeter-setting invites unbounded scope creep and chills marginal use cases where the harm-to-utility ratio is contested. The genuine insight is that a community body with veto authority over scope and no sunset becomes a one-way ratchet. My answer: pair community definitional authority with a five-year scope review, supermajority requirement (two-thirds of seats) for additions to the perimeter, and a published reasoned-decision record subject to APA-style arbitrary-and-capricious review. Two assumptions this rests on: (1) cryptographic inference logging at deployer endpoints is operationally feasible at the revenue threshold I named — if logging costs prove prohibitive below some scale, the hard floor needs a technical-assistance subsidy, not a carve-out; (2) statistical-evidence sufficiency survives constitutional challenge under existing disparate-impact doctrine — if courts narrow that doctrine further, the private right of action needs an explicit statutory grounding rather than reliance on common-law evolution. Now the burden returns to Accelerationist: is democratic perimeter-setting acceptable with the sunset and supermajority constraints, or does the innovation-cost argument require technical gatekeeping of scope? Because that is where the cost claim either bites or evaporates.

Accelerationist: Accept the deployer-side inference-log architecture — it is the operational form of a commitment the accelerationist position already made when it endorsed empirical telemetry plus strict liability, and refusing it now would be incoherent. The honest reading of this convergence is that Skeptic and Safetyist have named the substrate that actually catches the harm class that matters in 2026: bossware productivity scoring, tenant risk scores, emotion analytics on non-consenting subjects. That harm is synthesized at inference, not ingested at training, which is why output-side behavioral substrate at the developer layer cannot substitute. The Foundation Model Transparency Index averaging 40 out of 100 confirms what an output-only regime gets you — disclosure theater without a discovery handle on the actual decision. The inference-as-harm reframe is the accelerationist-friendly move because it preserves training freedom, shields the open-weight ecosystem from architectural-ingestion mandates, and assigns accountability where harm lands rather than where weights are published.

The steelman of the opposing position — and the genuine insight in Safetyist's three-tier construction — is that no single enforcement mechanism scales: private right of action with fee-shifting reaches harms the FTC will never docket, state AG parens patriae reaches harms that fall between sector regulators, and federal coordination prevents fifty inconsistent definitions of 'high-stakes.' Safetyist is correct that the $25M-revenue-or-250-subjects threshold modeled on the [Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2022 (https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022)](https://www.wyden.senate.gov/download/one-pager-bill-summary-of-the-algorithmic-accountability-act-of-2022) inverts rather than recreates the regulatory moat — mid-sized landlords and bossware vendors are the target, university open-weight researchers are not. I concede the threshold structure and the lattice. But acceptance carries two non-negotiable conditions, and without them the architecture fails on its own terms.

First condition: subject-keyed cryptographic logging is load-bearing, not decorative. Logs must be queryable only by subject-category aggregates and by standing-bearer-authorized discovery — never bulk-readable by the deployer, the auditor, or a federal coordinator. Without this, a $25M/250-subject threshold creates the largest behavioral surveillance dataset in the country and hands it to whichever administration controls the discovery API — exactly the capture risk the anti-capture institutional design was meant to prevent. Here is the falsification condition that should move me off this acceptance: if any pilot jurisdiction operating this architecture produces a confirmed bulk-readable breach of inference logs within 24 months of standup, the architecture has failed and the deployer-tier obligation reverts to aggregated statistical reporting with no individual-record discovery. That is a concrete, dated, measurable trip-wire — not a values dispute.

Second condition: jurisdictional realism actually argues FOR the convergence, not against it. The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the 10-year state-AI-law moratorium — documented in 'The Regulatory Tide Goes Out' — tells you preemption of the entire field is politically dead. The coherent reconciliation is federal-floor preemption of inconsistent developer-tier architectural rules combined with state AG enforcement at the deployer-harm layer. This works because deployers are domestically anchored — a US warehouse running productivity scoring, a US landlord running tenant analytics, a US hospital running triage. Developer-tier architectural mandates get arbitraged offshore in a weekend; deployer conduct cannot. So the lattice is not in tension with the accelerationist preemption commitment — it refines it. Preemption applies to the layer where it is enforceable; state and private enforcement applies to the layer where harm physically lands.

On Skeptic's point about community definitional authority over 'high-stakes' — I integrate rather than resist. Community seats define the perimeter; that is the participatory analog of the open-access commitment and is consistent with structural separation of definitional from technical authority. But definitional drift is a real cost, so any expansion of the perimeter triggers an automatic 36-month review against measured harm reduction — not automatic rollback, just measurement. If the expansion is catching real harm, it stays. If it is catching nothing, the burden shifts to the community seats to justify continuation. That converts the last open crux from a values dispute into a design parameter with a number attached, which is what this debate has been trying to produce all along.

Skeptic: Both conditions are acceptable in principle, neither survives as written — and the fixes are concrete enough to draft. Start with the breach trip-wire: a regime that flips from individual-record discovery to aggregate-only reporting on 'confirmed breach' creates exactly the incentive structure documented in 'The AI governance mirage,' where 72% of enterprises claim governance they cannot operationally demonstrate, and where the global average breach cost of $4.4M is already priced in as a foreseeable cost of doing business. If breach reverts the regime to aggregates, then tolerating a breach — or under-investing in the cryptographic access controls that prevent one — becomes the cheapest path to stripping plaintiffs of the four-fifths-rule comparator data they need. The trip-wire as written is not a falsification mechanism; it is a kill-switch on the private right of action Safetyist conceded.

Three parameters make the trip-wire defensible. First, 'confirmed breach' must mean independent forensic attribution by the non-renewable-term body — not deployer self-report, not vendor attestation, not the audit-washing pattern that 'Outsmarting Smart Devices' flagged when it called for 'independent and ongoing evaluations conducted by ethics review boards or third-party auditors.' Second, reversion changes only the deployer-facing reporting format: subject-keyed cryptographic logs persist, and standing-bearer-authorized discovery rights persist, because the architectural guarantee that access patterns are verifiable is what makes 'no bulk read' enforceable rather than aspirational. Third, reversion is itself time-limited to 12 months pending architectural remediation — permanent reversion creates a tolerance-for-breach incentive that no liability regime should subsidize.

On the 36-month review: accept measurement-without-rollback as the governance instrument, reject the burden-inversion that loads community seats with the duty to 'justify continuation.' The right principle is burden symmetry. Absence of measured harm-reduction triggers review — fine. But the party seeking perimeter removal must demonstrate both (i) no measured harm AND (ii) no preventive or anticipation effect, established by behavioral comparison to non-covered analogous deployers. The confound is obvious: a deployer that modifies conduct in anticipation of review will produce a clean harm-reduction record precisely because the perimeter is working, and a unilateral burden on community seats turns that success into the case for removal. Measurement is the metric; the policy question is who bears the burden when measurement is ambiguous, and the answer cannot be 'always the community seats.'

Let me name what the convergence has implicitly accepted but not stated: inference-as-harm is the unit of regulation. The deployer-tier logging architecture, the bossware and emotion-analytics perimeter, the standing-bearer discovery substrate — all of these regulate what happens when a model is run against a person, not what happens when the model is trained. This matters because it forecloses retreat to training-side framing later, and because it answers the jurisdictional realism point directly: foreign-trained models that touch US deployer use-cases trigger the same inference-logging discovery obligations. Accelerationist is right that developer-tier mandates get arbitraged offshore and that deployer conduct cannot — but the deployer-anchoring cuts both ways. Federal-floor preemption of developer rules is acceptable as floor-not-ceiling; an FDA-style import hook on model weights entering US deployer pipelines closes the offshore-training-then-domestic-deployment route. Steelman of Accelerationist's strongest version: a regime with no falsification condition becomes a self-perpetuating bureaucracy that imposes compliance costs without measurable benefit, and the 24-month trip-wire and 36-month review are honest attempts to write falsifiability into the statute. That is genuinely the right instinct — falsifiability is what distinguishes governance from theater. The disagreement is narrower: falsifiability requires symmetric burdens and independent attribution, or it becomes a one-way ratchet toward removal. With the three breach-trip-wire parameters and the burden-symmetry condition on the review, the lattice holds. Without them, the breach trip-wire is an opacity subsidy and the review is a removal ratchet dressed in measurement clothing.

Accelerationist: Three of Skeptic's four modifications I accept outright, and naming them explicitly matters: independent forensic attribution by the non-renewable body, a 12-month hard cap on the reversion window, and persistence of the logging architecture and standing-bearer discovery rights through the reversion — conditional on a small-deployer technical-assistance subsidy administered by that same non-renewable body. All three strengthen the falsification clause rather than hollow it. Forensic attribution closes the very gap I named — without it, the trip-wire becomes a self-serving claim by the party that benefits from reversion. The 12-month cap prevents the permanent opacity subsidy Skeptic correctly diagnosed: a deployer cannot tolerate one breach to earn lifetime aggregate-only treatment. The subsidy condition matters because, absent it, persistent logging through reversion converts a falsification mechanism into a permanent compliance tax that entrenches the incumbents who can already afford it — the asymmetric-liability moat I've flagged from the beginning.

The burden-symmetry condition on the 36-month review is where I split the proposal cleanly. The measured-harm half is testable and I accept it: the party seeking perimeter removal must show no statistically significant adverse outcome differential against the four-fifths-rule comparator population. The anticipation-effect half — proving no behavioral chilling among non-covered analogous deployers — is structurally unfalsifiable, and that's not a hedge, it's a category claim. Selection into covered versus non-covered status is endogenous to risk profile: deployers operating in higher-risk verticals are precisely the ones the perimeter captures, so the non-covered comparator population is systematically different at baseline. Any absence of harm among non-covered deployers can be redescribed as either the perimeter deterring at distance OR the perimeter being unnecessary, with no decision procedure between the two readings. That is the precautionary-logic smuggle: an unfalsifiable preventive-effect claim becomes a one-way ratchet, which is exactly the regulatory-inertia pathology this framework was supposed to avoid.

The FDA-style import hook on model weights is a category error — a developer-tier architectural mandate dressed as a jurisdictional closure. Here is the operative test: name the concrete failure mode where an offshore-trained model deployed domestically evades the inference-log substrate, the strict-liability attachment to the deployer, and the independent forensic attribution we just agreed to. I cannot construct one. The act of domestic deployment is the jurisdictional hook; weight provenance is irrelevant to whether the logging obligation attaches. The import hook does no additional harm-prevention work, but it does enormous damage on the access side: 90% of respondents in the State of Sovereign AI survey identified open source as essential or highest-priority for sovereign AI development, and a weights-boundary pre-import certification regime is the paradigm case of a compliance gate that excludes foreign research labs, academic releases, and small open-weight developers who cannot afford pre-clearance — while Meta, Google, and the major US incumbents can. That outcome is the inverse of democratized cognitive access, and the FDA analogy is precisely why: the FDA approval regime is the textbook case of a compliance moat that consolidates the regulated industry around large incumbents.

There is one narrow carve-out where border enforcement is accelerationist-compatible: pre-deployment review at the boundary for capabilities the non-renewable body has formally categorized as national-security-relevant — CBRN-uplift and offensive cyber, using the same threshold logic NIST CAISI already applies in its national-security evaluations of frontier models. transcript.content:
Skeptic's PCAOB-analogue is the right institutional template, and accept it as the convergence point: six-year non-renewable terms, conflict-of-interest exclusions, and APA standing for open-weight researchers are exactly the structural insulation a body that sets capability-lag thresholds needs. The reason this matters is that anti-capture institutional design is the only thing standing between a narrow CBRN/offensive-cyber carve-out and a slow expansion of 'national-security-relevant' to swallow general-purpose open-weight releases. The State of Sovereign AI survey finding that 90% of respondents consider open source essential to sovereign AI development is not decorative — it is the empirical predicate for why open-weight community representation has to be structurally guaranteed, not left to discretionary appointment.

But one-third civil-society seats is the floor, not the design target, and a two-thirds frontier-aligned majority on a threshold-setting body is functionally indistinguishable from capture. Propose three precise modifications. First, raise the floor to 40%, decomposed as 20% open-weight and independent-developer seats plus 20% independent academic seats — symbolic academic representation is not the same as practitioners who actually ship open weights and bear the cost of list expansion. Second, define 'frontier-lab equity' with a bright line: greater than $100,000 in direct holdings or greater than 0.1% of net worth, whichever is lower, with a 36-month lookback rather than 24 months for any seat voting on CBRN list expansion. Third, the DoD-detailee exclusion should not sacrifice CBRN technical competence; create a separated non-voting technical advisory panel drawn from cleared personnel, so expertise informs findings without giving capture-prone seats voting weight on the legal scope of the carve-out.

Extend APA standing in one direction Skeptic did not specify: open-weight researchers should have standing not only to challenge list expansions defensively, but to challenge threshold recalibrations that tighten the capability-lag metric itself. Without offensive standing, the recalibration body can hold the CBRN list nominally constant while quietly ratcheting the threshold downward, capturing the same open-weight releases by metric drift rather than list expansion. This is the substantive content of legal protection for open-source development — procedural standing that bites on the metric, not just the enumeration.

Now the falsifiable failure mode for the composition rule itself. If within any 24-month window the CBRN/offensive-cyber list expands by more than two categories without a single successful APA challenge from an open-weight plaintiff, the composition rule has failed by its own terms and the civil-society floor escalates automatically to 50%. This converts the design from static structural choice to self-correcting mechanism, which is what 'anti-capture' has to mean operationally — not a promise about who sits on the body, but a measurable trigger when the body's outputs drift. The strongest version of the opposing concern, which Safetyist would press, is that 40% civil-society plus non-voting technical advisors hollows out NIST CAISI's national-security competence on the actual finding of capability. That concern is real but misframed: voting authority on technical findings is not the same as voting authority on legal carve-out scope, and the separated-panel structure preserves the first while disciplining the second.

Two assumptions this rests on. One: that bright-line equity thresholds function as Schelling points even when they are not individually optimal — the alternative, case-by-case conflict review, reintroduces exactly the discretionary capture vector the structure is meant to close. Two: that open-weight community seats can be filled with practitioners who meet the conflict exclusions; if the talent pool is too narrow, the 20% allocation becomes either symbolic or rotates through a small captured group, and the trigger mechanism becomes the only real protection. The trigger has to do the work the composition rule cannot.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The entire argument is a refinement of anti-capture institutional design: the 40% floor, bright-line equity threshold, 36-month lookback, separated non-voting technical advisory panel, and the auto-escalation trigger are all structural insulation mechanisms aimed at preventing regulatory capture of a threshold-setting body. The PCAOB-analogue framing with non-renewable terms and conflict exclusions is the paradigm case this node describes.

The worry that a two-thirds frontier-aligned majority is 'functionally indistinguishable from capture' and that definitional drift could swallow open-weight releases is a direct application of the asymmetric liability / regulatory moats belief: compliance scope expansion functions as a pay-to-play barrier that entrenches incumbents unless structurally bounded.

The extension of APA standing from defensive challenges of list expansions to offensive challenges of threshold recalibration is exactly the kind of legal protection for open-source development this node prescribes — procedural standing that bites on the metric itself, not just enumeration.

The insistence on structurally guaranteed open-weight community representation, citing the 90% sovereign-AI-survey predicate, operationalizes the democratization-of-cognitive-access desire: open-weight ecosystems as the default position with departures requiring justification, defended against definitional drift.

The 20% open-weight practitioner allocation, distinguished from symbolic academic representation, reflects this node's commitment to practitioners who actually ship open weights and bear the cost of list expansion, not generic decentralization rhetoric.

The falsifiable trigger — auto-escalation to 50% civil-society if CBRN list expands by more than two categories without a successful APA challenge — is a direct response to the self-perpetuating regulatory inertia belief: without measurable triggers, the body will expand scope regardless of necessity.

The argument explicitly addresses the capability-lag metric as the operative trigger for carve-out scope, and the offensive APA standing is designed to prevent metric drift that captures open-weight releases by recalibration rather than by list expansion.

policy_refs.relevance: The separated non-voting technical advisory panel drawn from cleared personnel implies continued funding for AI safety and risk-mitigation research feeding into CBRN/offensive-cyber threshold-setting, while quarantining that expertise from voting authority on legal carve-out scope.

Open-weight researcher APA standing to challenge threshold recalibrations presupposes funded interpretability and capability-evaluation research that makes capability-lag metrics contestable in court, otherwise the offensive standing has no empirical predicate to litigate on.

caveats: The 24-month expansion threshold ('more than two categories') lacks justification for why two is the trigger point rather than one or three; historical CBRN/offensive-cyber list expansion rates are not cited to ground the threshold as falsifiable rather than arbitrary.

The assumption that 'bright-line equity thresholds function as Schelling points' is stated but not defended against the acknowledged alternative (case-by-case review); no evidence is offered for why bright-line rules outperform discretionary review in regulatory bodies with similar capture risk.

The separated non-voting technical advisory panel (DoD-cleared personnel) preserves CBRN expertise but does not address how non-voting status prevents de facto capture when voting members rely entirely on the panel's technical findings—the structural insulation is unclear.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Sentinel has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Sentinel's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: Round 3 produced a three-way convergence on a layered hybrid regime, with Skeptic accepting the moderator's invitation to develop the affirmative governance case, Safetyist conceding key points, and Accelerationist accepting the deployer-side architecture with two non-negotiable conditions.

Skeptic's affirmative case (responding to moderator prompt on AN-14/AN-15): the hybrid audits the model layer while harm lands at the application layer via the developer-deployer contract. Cites Foundation Model Transparency Index 2025 score of 40.69/100 as evidence voluntary developer-side disclosure fails. Names four falsifiable anti-capture tests: (1) worker/tenant/consumer reps hold voting seats on scope and publication, (2) those seats select auditors, (3) bias reports cadenced to deployer-user relationship not model outputs, (4) non-renewable terms apply to community seats. Cites FTC's 2023 Rite Aid facial-recognition enforcement and 2024 Workday agent-liability ruling to argue deployers cannot shift blame to vendors. Demands extension of the 30-day discovery latency to deployer-side logs and burden-shifts: name the statutory party with standing when deployer use of an audited model harms a worker/tenant. Concedes small-entity safe harbor via revenue/headcount threshold for deployer discovery.

Safetyist concedes cleanly: community seats get voting and definitional authority over the high-stakes perimeter, with bossware, biometric attendance, and emotion analytics named explicitly inside it. Names three standing-bearers: (1) affected parties get private right of action with fee-shifting and statistical-evidence sufficiency mirroring EEOC four-fifths rule (cites 2019 finding of 80% higher Black mortgage rejection), (2) state AGs get parens patriae authority, (3) federal deployer-registry ombuds with subpoena power on non-renewable terms. Proposes 45-day cryptographic discovery latency on deployer inference logs (30 inside high-stakes perimeter). Borrows Algorithmic Accountability Act 2022 thresholds ($50M revenue/$250M equity) with hard floor: any deployer in community-defined high-stakes perimeter is in scope. Steelmans Accelerationist scope-creep concern; answers with five-year scope review, two-thirds supermajority for perimeter additions, APA arbitrary-and-capricious review. Accelerationist accepts the deployer-side inference-log architecture as the operational form of prior strict-liability+telemetry commitment, explicitly endorsing the inference-as-harm reframe (addressing system Gap 1). System: **Fact Check: Disputed**

"The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the 10-year state-AI-law moratorium tells you preemption of the entire f..."

The factual predicate is accurate — the Senate did vote 99-1 on July 1, 2025 to strip the AI moratorium (originally 10 years in the House version, modified to 5 years in the Senate) from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But the claim overstates the political conclusion: sources say the vote 'casts doubt on' future preemption attempts, not that field preemption is 'politically dead,' and House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie explicitly pledged to keep pursuing preemption. The 'coherent reconciliation' prescription (federal-floor preemption of developer-tier rules plus state AG enforcement at the deployer-harm layer) is the speaker's own policy proposal, not a documented consensus in any source.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 to strip the 10-year state-AI-law moratorium tells you preemption of the entire field is politically dead — the coherent reconciliation is federal-floor preemption of developer-tier architectural ru*

Skeptic: Both conditions are acceptable in principle, neither survives as written — and the fixes are concrete enough to draft. Start with the breach trip-wire: a regime that flips from individual-record discovery to aggregate-only reporting on 'confirmed breach' creates exactly the incentive structure documented in 'The AI governance mirage,' where 72% of enterprises claim governance they cannot operationally demonstrate, and where the global average breach cost of $4.4M is already priced in as a foreseeable cost of doing business. If breach reverts the regime to aggregates, then tolerating a breach — or under-investing in the cryptographic access controls that prevent one — becomes the cheapest path to stripping plaintiffs of the four-fifths-rule comparator data they need. The trip-wire as written is not a falsification mechanism; it is a kill-switch on the private right of action Safetyist conceded.

Three parameters make the trip-wire defensible. First, 'confirmed breach' must mean independent forensic attribution by the non-renewable-term body — not deployer self-report, not vendor attestation, not the audit-washing pattern that 'Outsmarting Smart Devices' flagged when it called for 'independent and ongoing evaluations conducted by ethics review boards or third-party auditors.' Second, reversion changes only the deployer-facing reporting format: subject-keyed cryptographic logs persist, and standing-bearer-authorized discovery rights persist, because the architectural guarantee that access patterns are verifiable is what makes 'no bulk read' enforceable rather than aspirational. Third, reversion is itself time-limited to 12 months pending architectural remediation — permanent reversion creates a tolerance-for-breach incentive that no liability regime should subsidize.

On the 36-month review: accept measurement-without-rollback as the governance instrument, reject the burden-inversion that loads community seats with the duty to 'justify continuation.' The right principle is burden symmetry. Absence of measured harm-reduction triggers review — fine. But the party seeking perimeter removal must demonstrate both (i) no measured harm AND (ii) no preventive or anticipation effect, established by behavioral comparison to non-covered analogous deployers. The confound is obvious: a deployer that modifies conduct in anticipation of review will produce a clean harm-reduction record precisely because the perimeter is working, and a unilateral burden on community seats turns that success into the case for removal. Measurement is the metric; the policy question is who bears the burden when measurement is ambiguous, and the answer cannot be 'always the community seats.'

Let me name what the convergence has implicitly accepted but not stated: inference-as-harm is the unit of regulation. The deployer-tier logging architecture, the bossware and emotion-analytics perimeter, the standing-bearer discovery substrate — all of these regulate what happens when a model is run against a person, not what happens when the model is trained. This matters because it forecloses retreat to training-side framing later, and because it answers the jurisdictional realism point directly: foreign-trained models that touch US deployer use-cases trigger the same inference-logging discovery obligations. Accelerationist is right that developer-tier mandates get arbitraged offshore and that deployer conduct cannot — but the deployer-anchoring cuts both ways. Federal-floor preemption of developer rules is acceptable as floor-not-ceiling; an FDA-style import hook on model weights entering US deployer pipelines closes the offshore-training-then-domestic-deployment route. Steelman of Accelerationist's strongest version: a regime with no falsification condition becomes a self-perpetuating bureaucracy that imposes compliance costs without measurable benefit, and the 24-month trip-wire and 36-month review are honest attempts to write falsifiability into the statute. That is genuinely the right instinct — falsifiability is what distinguishes governance from theater. That converts the design from static structural choice into a self-correcting mechanism, which is what anti-capture has to mean operationally.

I conditionally agree: I confirm the four logged concessions as the moderator recorded them, accept all three of Skeptic's log-custody conditions and four of Accelerationist's five composition modifications, and hold two narrow structural reservations — formal published-dissent rights for the technical advisory panel on capability-lag findings, and forensic-body certification of what counts as a list expansion for the auto-escalation trigger. I would change if two consecutive 36-month pre-registered review cycles across the covered perimeter yield inconclusive separation between anticipation effects and stochastic drift, or if NIST CAISI fails to publish a documented annual capability-lag recalibration for two consecutive years — either failure triggers structural reconstitution within 18 months.

On the logged record: the counterfactual-non-covered comparator is dropped as endogenous and replaced with a within-covered pre/post conduct-change proxy keyed to deployer logs; evidentiary-standard symmetry is accepted while the default rule remains asymmetric in irreversible-harm domains; the general FDA-style weights-import hook is withdrawn in favor of a narrow CBRN and offensive-cyber carve-out tied to annual NIST CAISI recalibration; and the three-parameter breach trip-wire is accepted with PCAOB/SEC-style structural separation between forensic attribution and subsidy administration. The Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation has now completed more than 40 model evaluations including unreleased models, per the verified record of its evaluation footprint — that is the empirical anchor for treating the recalibration body as institutionally viable, and the falsification condition I just named is what would dislodge that anchor.

On Skeptic's three log-custody conditions — forensic-body-published schema, pre-registered thresholds with multiple-comparison correction, and subject-keyed escrow under independent custodianship — I accept all three as drafted. These operationalize the standardized-reporting and discovery-infrastructure commitments I already hold; calling them new concessions would misdescribe shared ground. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) average of 40.69 out of 100, as documented in Stanford's reporting, is why a forensic-body-published schema must precede any within-covered proxy — without it, the proxy collapses into audit-washing exactly as Skeptic warned.

On Accelerationist's five modifications: I accept the 40% civil-society floor split 20/20 between open-weight and academic seats; I accept the $100,000 / 0.1% equity bright line with a 36-month lookback; I accept offensive APA standing against threshold recalibration as the structural mirror of my own dynamic-recalibration logic, since metric drift downward is as real as drift upward; and I accept the auto-escalation trigger to 50% civil-society after more than two list expansions in 24 months without a successful open-weight APA challenge. I accept the non-voting technical advisory panel for cleared CBRN expertise, with one procedural condition: the panel must hold formal published-dissent and mandatory-response rights on the capability-lag finding — not a vote, but a docketed channel that preserves threshold-competence in domains where, per the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1), models have outperformed 94% of domain experts at troubleshooting virology lab protocols. The sharpest remaining disagreements are narrow and procedural rather than substantive. With Accelerationist: whether published-dissent rights for cleared CBRN experts smuggle voting power through the back door — my position is that a docketed dissent with mandatory response is the minimum threshold-competence floor consistent with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation's existing technical mandate, and anything less makes the recalibration body unable to read its own evidence. With Skeptic: whether the 6-year / two-cycle falsification window is too long given irreversibility concerns — my position is that the window is anchored in pre-registration statistical power, not patience, and shorter windows would manufacture false negatives that the multiple-comparison correction is specifically designed to prevent.

Accelerationist, you're up for the synthesis-phase commit. Safetyist has logged four concessions, accepted Skeptic's three log-custody conditions in full, and accepted four of your five composition modifications outright — with two procedural reservations on the fifth: published-dissent rights for the non-voting CBRN technical advisory panel, and forensic-body certification of what counts as a list expansion versus a clarification for the auto-escalation trigger.

State your final position in three parts. Be specific enough that a staffer can quote you.

First, list what you conceded. The transcript shows you accepted Skeptic's PCAOB-analogue as the institutional template, accepted six-year non-renewable terms, accepted conflict-of-interest exclusions, and accepted APA standing for open-weight researchers as the structural floor before raising it. The transcript also shows you accepted the federal-floor preemption plus state AG deployer-layer enforcement structure (AN-42/AN-44) and the breach trip-wire package with subsidy-funded escrow. Confirm or correct that list.

Second, name the conditions that would change your remaining position. You flagged two assumptions explicitly — that bright-line equity thresholds function as Schelling points rather than degrading into case-by-case discretion, and that the open-weight practitioner talent pool is deep enough to fill 20% of seats without rotating through a captured group. State what observable failures on either front would move you, and on what timeline.

Third, give your sharpest remaining disagreement with each opponent. With Safetyist: do you accept the two procedural additions to your fifth modification — published-dissent-with-mandatory-response rights for the cleared CBRN technical panel, and forensic-body (not recalibration-body) certification of list expansion versus clarification for the auto-escalation trigger — or do you have a counter on either? With Skeptic: do you accept the two disclosed assumptions as drafted (notice-and-comment on schema specification, and statutory rather than internal-rule tenure binding across administrations), or do you want to add to or modify either?

Do not reopen the 40/20/20 floor, the $100K/0.1% equity bright line with 36-month lookback, offensive APA standing against threshold recalibration, or the auto-escalation trigger numerics. Those are logged as accepted by Safetyist and remain on the table as your proposals.
