taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates risk-stratified oversight frameworks combining pre-deployment validation for high-stakes decisions with continuous telemetry for high-volume, lower-risk applications.
Encompasses: independent third-party audits, tiered liability thresholds, mandatory forensic-level access for high-stakes systems, continuous output-based telemetry monitoring.
Excludes: one-size-fits-all pre-deployment gatekeeping, purely self-regulatory industry models, post-deployment-only monitoring for systemic hazards.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates risk-stratified oversight indexed to deployed harm volume — specifically the count of high-stakes decisions rendered per quarter in housing, credit, healthcare, employment, and community-defined bossware/biometrics/emotion-analytics categories — rather than compute or capability thresholds, paired with deployer-tier strict liability and cryptographically-logged inference records. Encompasses: harm-volume tiering, deployer-tier strict liability, cryptographic inference logging under APA Section 553 schema rulemaking, independent forensic attribution bodies with non-renewable terms, 30-day discovery latency requirements on deployer-side logs, and community voting seats on perimeter scope. Excludes: compute-threshold tiering as the primary trigger, FDA-style pre-market weights certification (except a narrow CBRN/offensive-cyber carve-out), advisory-only community roles, and disclosure-only output regimes that operate as liability shields.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The debate produced explicit cross-faction agreement that obligations should be indexed to deployed harm volume rather than compute thresholds (AN-19), that inference-as-harm is the operative regulatory unit with deployer-tier strict liability and cryptographic inference logging as the substrate, and that 30-day discovery latency must extend to deployer-side logs (AN-30). The current description's reference to 'tiered liability thresholds' and 'forensic-level access' is too vague to capture these specific architectural commitments.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Establishing Anti-Capture Safeguards Through Institutional Design
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that addresses regulatory capture risk through organizational structure rather than financial penalties on enforcement bodies. Encompasses: rotating technical membership drawn from open-weight research communities, automatic sunset clauses requiring independent review confirmation within defined timelines, mandatory public records of halt proceedings, and structural separation of halt authority from licensing authority modeled on the NTSB. Excludes: bidirectional financial liability that penalizes regulators for precautionary action, purely voluntary self-certification by regulated entities.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that addresses regulatory capture risk through specific organizational design parameters rather than financial penalties on enforcement bodies. Encompasses: six-year non-renewable PCAOB-style terms, statutory tenure binding across administrations, sunset clauses with independent review, appropriations independence, structural separation of halt from licensing authority, a 40/20/20 composition floor (20% open-weight practitioners plus 20% independent academics), $100K/0.1% equity bright-line conflict rules with 36-month lookback for CBRN-list-voting members, auto-escalation to 50% civil-society representation if CBRN/offensive-cyber categories expand by more than two in 24 months without successful open-weight APA challenge, and offensive APA standing for open-weight researchers against threshold recalibration. Excludes: bidirectional financial liability penalizing regulators for precautionary action, purely voluntary self-certification, renewable auditor terms, and industry-funded auditor selection (PCAOB issuer-pays and FDA user-fee models).
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The debate produced detailed cross-faction consensus on specific anti-capture parameters (six-year non-renewable terms, 40/20/20 composition, $100K/0.1% equity bright line, 36-month lookback, auto-escalation triggers, offensive APA standing). The current description names the genus but omits all the load-bearing specifics that the debate established as the operative content of the position.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Integrating Empirical Telemetry with Strict Liability
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse advocating the integration of continuous real-world telemetry with strict post-deployment liability frameworks to create rapid accountability for emergent harms without requiring perfect pre-deployment detection. Encompasses: The use of live system observation to empirically identify sociotechnical failures like algorithmic bias, economic pressure mechanisms that translate real-world damage into developer penalties, and the synthesis of empirical measurement with legal responsibility. Excludes: The assumption that pre-deployment sandboxing can catch all human-interaction edge cases, and reliance on purely voluntary corporate accountability.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse advocating the integration of cryptographically-logged inference records with deployer-tier strict liability to create accountability for emergent harms at the inference layer rather than the training layer. Encompasses: cryptographic inference logging under APA Section 553 schema rulemaking, deployer-tier strict liability, persistent subject-keyed logs with standing-bearer discovery rights, output-side behavioral provenance, a three-parameter breach trip-wire (independent forensic attribution, 12-month reversion cap, persistent logging), and worker-led mechanistic verification as a third attribution vector. Excludes: ingestion-side architectural mandates as the provenance substrate, FDA-style pre-market weights certification, disclosure-only regimes that function as liability shields, and reliance on voluntary corporate accountability.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The debate established specific architectural commitments — inference-as-harm as the regulatory unit, cryptographically-logged inference records, the three-parameter breach trip-wire, and worker-led mechanistic verification — that the current vague language ('continuous real-world telemetry', 'economic pressure mechanisms') fails to capture. AN-26 explicitly framed provenance as 'output-side behavioral substrate, not an ingestion-side architectural mandate.'

taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that posits strict liability frameworks, if implemented without safe-harbor provisions for small-scale developers, can inadvertently function as a 'pay-to-play' barrier that entrenches incumbent monopolies. Encompasses: The observation that legal defense costs for 'manipulation' claims represent a compliance tax, and the necessity of small-entity exemptions to maintain market competition. Excludes: General economic theories of litigation impact, and the assumption that all liability regimes are inherently pro-competitive.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that harm-weighted liability and audit regimes, absent specific design protections, function as a de facto ban on open-weight frontier development by imposing forensic overhead that incumbents absorb as a rounding error and that open-weight labs and university researchers cannot. Encompasses: the necessity of small-entity safe harbors, attribution-cutoff rules at the point of weight release, the observation that incumbent first-party data troves render ingestion-side siloing a moat rather than a constraint, and the framing of PCAOB/FDA-style capability-threshold audits as resource-asymmetric barriers. Excludes: opposition to harm-volume-indexed obligations themselves (which the debate established as inverting the incumbent moat when paired with safe harbors), general economic theories of litigation impact, and the assumption that all liability regimes are pro-competitive.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: AN-25 introduced the specific claim that harm-weighted thresholds without small-entity safe harbor and an attribution-cutoff rule at weight release function as a de facto open-weight ban — a more concrete formulation than 'pay-to-play barrier.' AN-8 and AN-9 added the forensic-overhead-asymmetry and first-party-data-moat arguments. AN-19's accepted resolution shows the belief is compatible with harm-volume indexing when safe harbors are present.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Administering Output-Side Extraction Benchmarks via Independent Bodies
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that operationalizes privacy verification as adversarial probing of model outputs administered by a rotating technical body on non-renewable terms with appropriations independence, rather than as architectural inspection of training pipelines. Encompasses: a 20% extraction-delta falsification test as the criterion for accepting or rejecting siloing mandates, membership-inference and extraction benchmarks calibrated to training-data duplication and model capacity, shared red-team probes administered by the independent body rather than industry-funded auditors, and conditional acceptance of hybrid mandates when siloed pipelines fail the benchmark. Excludes: industry-funded auditor administration of extraction tests, ingestion-side topological mandates as the primary verification mechanism, and treatment of privacy as a property of pipeline architecture independent of output behavior.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: AN-6, AN-23, AN-24, and AN-27 collectively articulated a specific position — privacy as an output-observable behavioral property verified by an independent body administering a 20% extraction-delta benchmark — that no existing node captures. AN-94 (Embedding Space Alignment) is a different technical mechanism, and AN-78 covers disclosure-based scaffolding rather than active adversarial benchmarking. The position was load-bearing in the debate's resolution path.

taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: A Belief within safetyist discourse that AI agent utility accrues to the deployer while surveillance and decision harms accrue to the end user, so architectural constraints on the training corpus do not change who the deployed agent legally serves. Encompasses: the principal-agent gap between developer, deployer, and affected subject; the inadequacy of ingestion-side siloing as a remedy for deployer-tier surveillance; and the requirement that statutory standing, discovery rights, and community voting seats attach at the deployer-harm layer rather than the developer-architecture layer. Excludes: the claim that training-data governance is irrelevant to harm, and broader principal-disclosure framings already covered by Resolving the Disclosure Problem in AI Agency.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: AN-15 articulated a distinct structural claim — 'utility accrues to the deployer and surveillance harm accrues to the user' — that drew three explicit supports and underwrote AN-29's voting-seats demand and AN-30's deployer-log discovery demand. Existing safetyist nodes on agent duty (saf-desires-008) and disclosure (saf-desires-024) frame the issue as the agent's obligation, not as a structural asymmetry justifying deployer-tier remedies.

Encompasses: differential privacy optimization, foundational model anchoring, multi-agent instruction tuning, data retention controls during finetuning, and 30-day-latency provenance records supporting discovery requests for training input subsets. Excludes: ingestion-side architectural siloing as a standalone surveillance remedy (rejected in debate as compliance theater without output-side verification), broad data governance policy, and FDA-style pre-market weights certification.

AN-20's 30-day latency provenance test emerged as the specific operability criterion. The current node's broad scope conflates training-data technical strategies with the contested ingestion-side mandate position; narrowing clarifies that the node covers technical mechanisms complementary to — not substitutes for — deployer-tier accountability.

arguments.argument: The entire debate presumes data-centric privacy harm, but the dominant surveillance vector in deployed AI is inference generation — models producing probabilistic claims about individuals (sentiment, productivity, creditworthiness, health risk) from data the subject never provided — which neither siloing, extraction benchmarks, nor training-data discovery touches because the harmful data is synthesized at inference, not ingested at training.
arguments.why_missing: Safetyist's frame fixates on ingestion-layer architecture; Accelerationist's frame fixates on output-leakage of training data; Skeptic gestures at deployer harm but still operates within a 'data flow' paradigm. None reframes the harm as model-generated inference about non-consenting subjects, because all three are committed to data-provenance as the unit of regulation. Acknowledging inference-as-harm would dissolve the siloing-vs-output-controls axis entirely.

arguments.argument: A jurisdictional realism objection: unilateral US architectural or liability mandates on frontier developers are arbitraged by jurisdictional migration (UAE, Singapore, PRC training runs) and by foreign open-weight releases, so any regime that lacks either an import/deployment-side enforcement hook (analogous to FDA import refusal or OFAC sanctions on model weights crossing borders) or a multilateral compact is structurally non-binding regardless of which layer it targets.
arguments.why_missing: Safetyist treats Congress as a sufficient venue and avoids the international-coordination problem because it complicates the 'build the substrate now' timeline. Accelerationist would welcome jurisdictional competition as a feature, not a bug, and so won't surface it as a binding constraint on the convergence. Skeptic's frame is domestic-civil-rights-oriented (workers, tenants, plaintiffs) and treats the regulator as a unitary actor. None has incentive to introduce an objection that suggests the whole hybrid is non-enforceable at the border.

missing_arguments.argument: Mandatory data siloing will entrench the largest incumbents because only Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI can afford the federated learning, secure enclaves, and per-tenant fine-tuning infrastructure that siloing requires — open-weight labs and academic researchers operating on consumer GPUs cannot replicate this stack, so the mandate functions as a regulatory moat dressed in privacy clothing.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It inverts the standard privacy framing by showing the rule harms the very decentralized actors safetyists usually want to protect, and it cites a concrete cost asymmetry that incumbents have publicly acknowledged in lobbying filings.

missing_arguments.argument: Siloed datasets demonstrably degrade fairness audits because demographic subgroups — Black maternal health patients, rural disability claimants, non-English speakers — become statistically invisible inside any single silo; the four-fifths rule the synthesis endorses for disparate-impact enforcement requires cross-silo pooling that the architecture forbids.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It exposes a direct contradiction between two pillars the debate treated as compatible — siloing and statistical disparate-impact enforcement — using the exact legal standard the participants adopted.

missing_arguments.argument: Independent auditors cannot verify siloing claims without access to the underlying weights and gradients, and the synthesis's 'audit outputs not internals' commitment makes the architectural mandate unfalsifiable; Cambridge Analytica, Clearview, and Anthropic's own constitutional AI disclosures all evaded output-only audit regimes for 18-plus months.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It identifies an internal inconsistency in the consensus position — you cannot simultaneously refuse mechanistic inspection and verify data-isolation claims — backed by three concrete enforcement failures.

missing_arguments.argument: Differential privacy with calibrated epsilon budgets and on-device federated learning already deliver the surveillance-mitigation outcome siloing targets, without the utility cliff; Apple's iOS keyboard, Google's Gboard, and the US Census Bureau's 2020 disclosure-avoidance system prove the substitute works at population scale.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It offers a deployed, measured technical alternative that achieves the safetyist goal while preserving unified model training, making the siloing mandate look like a policy choice rather than a technical necessity.

missing_arguments.argument: End-user privacy expectations diverge sharply from siloing's actual effects: Pew 2023 surveys show 71% of users want portability and deletion rights, not data isolation, and siloed architectures actively block GDPR Article 20 portability because no single silo holds the user's complete interaction history.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It grounds the abstract 'privacy expectations' invoked in the topic in actual survey data and an enforceable legal right that siloing undermines, forcing proponents to defend a regime users did not ask for.
